name: Símákonde
confidence_why: 6 independent first-hand descriptions agree (3 state the same rule, 2 refine it). One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Manus 2010.
catalog_citation: Manus, Sophie. 2010. The Prosody of Símákonde Relative Clauses. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 53: 159-185 (Papers from the Workshop on Bantu Relative Clauses). Open-access PDF, zaspil.leibniz-zas.de article 388.
catalog_locator: sec. 3.1 'Stress', p.161 (also abstract p.159); examples (1) p.162
catalog_quote: Like other Makonde dialects and other Eastern and Southern Bantu languages (Hyman 2009), Símákonde has lost the historical Proto-Bantu vowel length contrast and now has a regular phrase-final stress rule, which causes a predictable lengthening of the penultimate syllable of every Prosodic Phrase. The penult lengthened by stress is bimoraic. ... Examples in (1) show penultimate lengthening in Símákonde. (1) a. kúlúúma 'to bite' b. kúlúmúúla 'to cut' c. kúlúmúláánga 'to cut into small pieces' d. kúlúmúlángííla 'to cut into small pieces for someone'
sweep_summary: Four title-keyword items for Makonde (mako1251, catalog 'phrasal' on Manus 2010). Read: (1) Liphola 1991 UNICAMP MA thesis — newly located and downloaded open from the UNICAMP Sophia repository (scanned PDF with text, saved); it separates predictable, optional pre-pausal penultimate lengthening (no length contrast) from 'acento de intensidade', which it equates with High tone and describes as variable in position; refines the catalog (confirms the pause-final penult lengthening, questions calling it stress). (2) Philippson 1991 thesis (already held by the project, copied into the folder): §3.9 and p. 358 n. 1 — Makonde has a demarcative accent realized as penultimate lengthening before absolute pause, no length contrast; confirms. Not read: (3) Liphola 1992 LASU proceedings — print only (OCLC 29617455), medium priority; (4) Liphola 2001 OSU dissertation — no open copy located (OhioLINK search form refused scripted queries; Kraal 2005 (ch. 3, p. 35, held by the project) summarizes it as treating penultimate lengthening as stress-driven and realized only utterance-finally, consistent with the phrasal coding. Also read held by the project: Leach 2010 §9.3.2 p. 330 (penultimate length marks the phonological-phrase boundary; confirms). Best new first-hand statement: Liphola 1991 pp. 31-32 and 115; it does not supersede Manus 2010 as the deciding source.

new_statements.quote: Em SMAK, o alongamento vocálico não é distintivo, uma vez que é predizível. A vogal longa, quando ocorre, tem quase sempre lugar na penúltima sílaba que antecede a pausa. Sua realização na língua é facultativa. Pelo contrário, o tom, a intensidade e os padrões tonais têm função distintiva. (pp. 31-32) [...] 1. O tom alto coincide sempre com o acento de intensidade. 2. A última sílaba (que antecede a pausa) não recebe tom, a menos que seja marcado no léxico. (p. 115)
new_statements.translation: In Si-Makonde, vowel lengthening is not distinctive, since it is predictable. The long vowel, when it occurs, almost always falls on the penultimate syllable preceding the pause. Its realization in the language is optional. By contrast, tone, stress and the tonal patterns have a distinctive function. [...] 1. High tone always coincides with stress. 2. The last syllable (preceding the pause) receives no tone unless it is lexically marked.
new_statements.citation: Liphola, Marcelino Marta. 1991. Tom, entonação e acento de intensidade na língua Si-Makonde: bases para um estudo morfotonológico. MA dissertation, IEL, Universidade Estadual de Campinas.
new_statements.locator: §3.2 'Vogal longa', pp. 31-32 (pp. 45-46); §6.2 principle 1, p. 115 (p. 131); conclusion p. 127 (p. 144)
new_statements.reading: A native-speaker first-hand description that keeps the two candidate 'stress' correlates apart: predictable, optional penultimate lengthening before pause (a phrase/pause-level phenomenon, no length contrast) versus 'acento de intensidade', which Liphola equates with the H-toned syllable and therefore treats as lexically variable in position (first, second, penult or last syllable, p. 127). It confirms the pre-pausal penultimate-lengthening rule behind the catalog's 'phrasal' coding but does not support calling the penult the stressed syllable in the word-stress sense; under Liphola's terminology Makonde is a tone language whose prominence tracks H, with intonational penult lengthening at pause.

tone_statements.citation: Rolle, Nicholas & Larry M. Hyman. 2019. Phrase-level prosodic smothering in Makonde. In Supplemental Proceedings of the 2018 Annual Meeting on Phonology (Proceedings of the Annual Meetings on Phonology 7). Washington, DC: LSA. 12 pp. [Also as UC Berkeley PhonLab Annual Report 14 (2018), DOI 10.5070/P7141042473.]
tone_statements.quote: Vowel length in Makonde is not contrastive. Instead, in all dialects surveyed Makonde shows phrase-level penultimate lengthening, an areal trend among Bantu languages that have lost the Proto-Bantu vowel length contrast (Hyman 2013). ... The examples in (2a-c) show that nouns and verbs in isolation bear non-contrastive penultimate lengthening (regardless of internal morphology), as in isolation they constitute a phonological phrase. ... [fn.3] Besides the effect on vowel length, demonstratives have the property of assigning all H tone to all words that precede it, corroborating the formation of a single φ domain.
tone_statements.locator: sec.2 'Phonological phrases in Makonde', p.2 of the AMP paper, and footnote 3 (p.4)
tone_statements.summary: H-toned vs toneless marking presupposed (H marked with acute); phrase-level H assignment before demonstratives; prominence = non-contrastive penultimate lengthening of each phonological phrase (a word in isolation is a phrase); no word-stress claim made.

tone_statements.citation: Patin, Cédric and Rialland, Annie (2006). On the nature of rules sensitive to syntax: the case of Makonde tonology. In Prosody and syntax: cross-linguistic perspectives. Amsterdam: John Benjamins Publ. pp. 285-301.
tone_statements.quote: in four dialects of Makonde, a Bantu language from East Africa: Simakonde [SIM], a dialect spoken by Makonde people who emigrated on the Zanzibar Island and in Tanga (Western Tanzania) – using data from Manus 2003 … In Simakonde, the rules are different. In a noun phrase with a demonstrative, the noun, whatever its lexical tones, is totally high: … This floating high tone has been found regularly in all the dialects of Makonde and was posited in all analysis of these dialects.
tone_statements.summary: Nouns carry lexical high vs low tones; a floating high tone (possessive) in all Makonde dialects; in Simakonde a noun before a demonstrative is all-high. Penult is the accented, lengthened syllable.

tone_statements.citation: Liphola, Marcelino Marta (2001). Aspects of Phonology and Morphology of Shimakonde. Ann Arbor: UMI. Ohio State University. xx+453 pp.
tone_statements.quote: On the surface, Shimakonde has H and L tones. Rising, falling, rise-fall and fall-rise contours occur in the language, but only on long vowels. Like in all other Bantu languages of zone P, Shimakonde lacks lexical tone contrasts in the verb stem. … What makes Shimakonde be tonally different in terms of tense-determined tone is the occurrence of the contours, which allow a four-way phonological tone contrast in verbs, as a way of marking tense-aspect mostly realized on the penult syllable
tone_statements.locator: pp. 202-203, §6.1 General Tone Principles (Ch. 6 Verbal Tonology); noun contrast at p. 377 §7.2 ex. (7.12)
tone_statements.summary: H vs L tones on moras; contours only on long (stressed penult) vowels. Verb tone is tense-determined, nouns have a five-way lexical penult tone contrast; separate penultimate stress with lengthening.

tone_statements.citation: Liphola, Marcelino Marta. 1991. Tom, entonação e acento de intensidade na língua Si-Makonde: bases para um estudo morfotonológico. MA dissertation, IEL, Universidade Estadual de Campinas.
tone_statements.quote: Os dados que temos vindo a analisar mostram que, embor~ existam variações de padrões tonais em SMAK, identificadas como ''variantes'' ou idiossincrasias, é possível distinguir dois níveis melódicos; alto e baixo. O termo ''nível melódico baixo'' é usado aqui não associado ao tom baixo, mas para indicar simplesmente a ausência de tom. … os níveis melódicos alto e baixo serem lexical- mente contrastivos, o que permite agrupar o léxico da língua em cerca de cinco padrões obtidos através de associação dos níveis melódicos acima referidos <ver exemplos 60-64).
tone_statements.translation: The data we have been analysing show that, although there are variations of tonal patterns in SMAK, identified as 'variants' or idiosyncrasies, it is possible to distinguish two melodic levels: high and low. The term 'low melodic level' is used here not associated with a low tone, but simply to indicate the absence of tone. … [crucially, in SMAK] the high and low melodic levels are lexically contrastive, which allows the lexicon of the language to be grouped into about five patterns obtained by association of the above melodic levels (see examples 60-64).
tone_statements.locator: p. 118, Cap. V sec. 6.3 'Sobre os níveis melódicos da língua SMAK'
tone_statements.summary: Two lexically contrastive melodic levels, high vs low (low = absence of tone), about five tonal patterns on radicals; contour tones derived, not basic; high tone always carries the stress accent.

tone_statements.citation: Philippson, Gérard. 1991. Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale: étude comparative typologique et diachronique. Thèse de doctorat d'État, Université Paris V (René Descartes). 542 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Le makonde est une langue à accent, qui n'est pas sans rappeler le matuumbi. [...] Le makonde connaît un accent démarcatif réalisé comme un allongement de la pénultième devant pause absolue. Il n'y a pas dans cette langue d'opposition de longueur vocalique. [...] c) langues à culmination de longueur, mais non de hauteur, sur la pénultième (langues à prosodèmes distinctifs, mais sans opposition de longueur) : [...] makonde [fn. 2: Il faut préciser que la très grande majorité des mots makonde (formes verbales ou nominales) ont, en fait, également une culmination de hauteur sur la pénultième et cette langue pourrait rentrer dans la première catégorie, n'étaient un petit nombre d'exceptions.]
tone_statements.translation: Makonde is an accent language, not unlike Matuumbi. [...] Makonde has a demarcative accent realised as lengthening of the penultimate before absolute pause. There is no vowel-length opposition in this language. [...] c) languages with culmination of length, but not of pitch, on the penultimate (languages with distinctive prosodemes but without a length opposition): [...] Makonde [fn. 2: It should be said that the great majority of Makonde words (verbal or nominal forms) in fact also have a pitch culmination on the penultimate, and this language could go into the first category (languages without distinctive prosodemes), were it not for a small number of exceptions.]
tone_statements.locator: section 3.9 'Le makonde (dialecte maraba)' p.356 with footnote 1 p.357; typology of penultimate culmination pp.483-484 footnote 2
tone_statements.summary: Restricted, accent-like H tone system (Philippson's 'langue à accent'): distinctive H prosodemes exist but almost every word has its pitch peak on the penult; demarcative accent = phrase-final penultimate lengthening; no vowel-length contrast (stated for Chimaraba Makonde, applied by Philippson to 'l'ensemble des dialectes makonde', not verified for Machinga).

tone_statements.citation: Odden, David [Arnold] (1990). Tone in the Makonde dialects: Chimahuta. Studies in African linguistics 21. pp. 149-187.
tone_statements.quote: Verbs have no lexical tone contrasts, and any tones appearing at the surface are assigned by rule. Every verb stem is assigned a single floating H tone by a rule … The stem H is then mapped to the penultimate syllable by one of three rules. … Nouns which become toneless due to their nominal construction reject the verbal H tone, just as lexically H toned nouns do. … the Chimahuta dialect has no contrast between rising tone and level H. Phonetically, the only opposition is between fall and H. This is due to a late rule, (3), spreading H leftward within the syllable.
tone_statements.summary: Chimahuta Makonde: H vs toneless, tones linked to moras; verbs have no lexical tone (stem H placed by rule), nouns lexically H-toned or toneless; surface fall vs level H only; penultimate stress.

sources.note: Native-speaker MA thesis. Separates three prosodic properties: tone (pitch), 'acento de intensidade' (stress = the most prominent syllable) and vowel lengthening (treated as intonational). (i) Vowel length is non-distinctive and predictable; the long vowel 'almost always' falls on the penultimate syllable before pause, its realization is optional ('facultativa'), and with CV+V+CV structures it can fall on the antepenult (pp. 31-35; rule p. 35: penult, or antepenult if V2 is long). sources.citation: Odden, David. 1990. Tone in the Makonde dialects: Chimaraba. Studies in African Linguistics 21(1): 61-105. Open access, journals.flvc.org/sal/article/view/107439.
sources.quote: p.63: 'there are no vowel length contrasts, but due to a regular stress rule, the penultimate syllable of every word is lengthened.' p.64: final syllable extraprosodic, 'stress is assigned to the final [visible, i.e. penultimate] syllable. Then, the stressed syllable is lengthened by (4) Stress Lengthening ... Stress with lengthening in utterance-medial words is not phonetically obvious, like utterance-final stress is, and is wiped out or severely reduced by a late postlexical rule.'

sources.citation: Leach, Michael Benjamin. 2010. Things hold together: foundations for a systemic treatment of verbal and nominal tone in Plateau Shimakonde. PhD dissertation, Universiteit Leiden (LOT 260). [Not a title-works with stress in the title; held by the project from the 2026-09-16 check; read here for the stress statement.]
sources.quote: p.330: 'Penultimate length is assigned non-contrastively in Plateau Shimakonde to mark the boundary of the phonological phrase.' sec.9.5: 'Following previous descriptions of Makonde, we find that the phonological phrase is defined by penultimate lengthening and is the domain within which lexical and grammatical tone assignment takes place.' T9.19/T9.25: lengthening on verb and complement in disjoint constructions, only on the complement in conjoint ones.
sources.note: First-hand fieldwork description of Plateau Shimakonde (Mozambique). No length contrast (§2.1, p. 26); penultimate length is assigned non-contrastively to the penultimate syllable of the phonological phrase, making it bimoraic (§2.2, pp. 26-27; §9.3.2, p. 330); conjoint verbs before a complement lack it, disjoint verbs and complements both get it (T9.19); it applies even when H tone falls on the final syllable (T9.20). Leach does not use the word 'stress' for it. Confirms the catalog's phrasal coding (phrase-final penult lengthening).

tone.quote: Vowel length in Makonde is not contrastive. Instead, in all dialects surveyed Makonde shows phrase-level penultimate lengthening, an areal trend among Bantu languages that have lost the Proto-Bantu vowel length contrast (Hyman 2013). ... The examples in (2a-c) show that nouns and verbs in isolation bear non-contrastive penultimate lengthening (regardless of internal morphology), as in isolation they constitute a phonological phrase. ... [fn.3] Besides the effect on vowel length, demonstratives have the property of assigning all H tone to all words that precede it, corroborating the formation of a single φ domain.
tone.locator: sec.2 'Phonological phrases in Makonde', p.2 of the AMP paper, and footnote 3 (p.4)
tone.summary: H-toned vs toneless marking presupposed (H marked with acute); phrase-level H assignment before demonstratives; prominence = non-contrastive penultimate lengthening of each phonological phrase (a word in isolation is a phrase); no word-stress claim made.
tone.says: Secondary analysis of phonological phrasing: vowel length non-contrastive, every phonological phrase marked by penultimate lengthening; whether N+modifier form one or two phrases is lexically idiosyncratic ('prosodic smothering'); demonstratives assign H tone to all preceding words in their phrase (fn.3); further tonal differences between 1-phrase and 2-phrase groupings explicitly set aside (fn.1). Confirms the catalog's phrase-penult prominence; says little about the tone inventory itself.

tone.quote: On the surface, Shimakonde has H and L tones. Rising, falling, rise-fall and fall-rise contours occur in the language, but only on long vowels. Like in all other Bantu languages of zone P, Shimakonde lacks lexical tone contrasts in the verb stem. … What makes Shimakonde be tonally different in terms of tense-determined tone is the occurrence of the contours, which allow a four-way phonological tone contrast in verbs, as a way of marking tense-aspect mostly realized on the penult syllable

tone.quote: Verbs have no lexical tone contrasts, and any tones appearing at the surface are assigned by rule. Every verb stem is assigned a single floating H tone by a rule … The stem H is then mapped to the penultimate syllable by one of three rules. … Nouns which become toneless due to their nominal construction reject the verbal H tone, just as lexically H toned nouns do. … the Chimahuta dialect has no contrast between rising tone and level H. Phonetically, the only opposition is between fall and H. This is due to a late rule, (3), spreading H leftward within the syllable.
tone.summary: Chimahuta Makonde: H vs toneless, tones linked to moras; verbs have no lexical tone (stem H placed by rule), nouns lexically H-toned or toneless; surface fall vs level H only; penultimate stress.

tone.quote: in four dialects of Makonde, a Bantu language from East Africa: Simakonde [SIM], a dialect spoken by Makonde people who emigrated on the Zanzibar Island and in Tanga (Western Tanzania) – using data from Manus 2003 … In Simakonde, the rules are different. In a noun phrase with a demonstrative, the noun, whatever its lexical tones, is totally high: … This floating high tone has been found regularly in all the dialects of Makonde and was posited in all analysis of these dialects.
tone.summary: Nouns carry lexical high vs low tones; a floating high tone (possessive) in all Makonde dialects; in Simakonde a noun before a demonstrative is all-high. Penult is the accented, lengthened syllable.
